analysis.one_liner: Slams the door on corporate tax shelters by denying tax breaks for deals with no real business purpose.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 52 House members, never left the Ways and Means Committee and died without a vote when the 109th Congress ended in January 2007.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have written the "economic substance" rule into law: a tax break only counts if the deal changes your real economic position and has a genuine purpose beyond taxes. It raised penalties for big companies, wealthy individuals, and tax preparers who hide or push abusive shelters, required advisors to disclose who buys them, and stopped corporations from gaming stock acquisitions and foreign-subsidiary rules to dodge taxes.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers, who otherwise bear the cost of the revenue lost to corporate tax shelters and of a tax system that feels less fair when sophisticated players avoid taxes others pay

how_it_helps.text: A tax break would be denied unless the deal meaningfully changed the taxpayer's economic position and had a substantial non-tax purpose, shutting down transactions set up only to manufacture deductions [S2][S3].
Penalties for failing to disclose tax shelters would rise to $100,000–$200,000 for large entities (over $10 million in receipts) and individuals with net worth over $2 million [S2][S3].

Understatements from transactions lacking economic substance would draw a 40% penalty (20% if disclosed), and advisors would have to disclose the identity of shelter clients, which could not be kept confidential [S2][S3].
Return preparers would face tougher standards and penalties up to $5,000 per improper understatement, and frivolous tax submissions would carry a $5,000 penalty [S2][S3].

The Treasury Secretary would gain broader power to disallow tax benefits from stock and property acquisitions made mainly to dodge taxes, plus new limits on foreign-corporation and dividend-basis games [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Large corporations, high-net-worth individuals, tax shelter promoters, and the accounting and law firms that design and justify these deals; small businesses or investors who used aggressive structures would also face tougher penalty exposure
analysis.who_pays_short: Large corporations, the wealthy, and shelter promoters

drawbacks.text: The frivolous-submission penalty would jump tenfold, from $500 to $5,000, and the IRS could dismiss frivolous hearing requests outright — a burden that falls on tax protesters, some of them low-income, rather than on corporate shelters [S3].

Writing the economic substance test into statute and raising the preparer standard to "more likely than not" would add compliance costs and legal uncertainty for some legitimate business transactions that depend on judgment calls about a deal's business purpose [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core of the bill — taxing deals by what they actually do rather than what they claim — addresses a real revenue and fairness problem that ordinary taxpayers pay for. Its heaviest penalties aim squarely at large entities and wealthy individuals. The main costs are higher compliance costs for some legitimate deals and a steep penalty increase aimed at tax protesters, a smaller group; on balance the design is sound, though the frivolous-submission provision is a blunt instrument.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the Ways and Means Committee from the day it was introduced until the 109th Congress ended — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote.

narrative.text: Lloyd Doggett of Texas introduced the bill on May 25, 2005, with 52 original cosponsors — 51 Democrats and one Independent — and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means [S1][S3][S4][S5].
That referral was the last action ever taken; the bill never received a committee vote or a floor vote and died when the Congress ended on January 3, 2007 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Promoters and users of abusive tax shelters — large corporations and wealthy individuals, along with the advisors who profit from selling them — were better off because the bill died; ordinary taxpayers kept bearing the revenue losses shelters cause.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Shelter promoters and their wealthy clients

for.name: Rep. Lloyd Doggett
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 52 original cosponsors; served on the Ways and Means Committee itself

against.name: Rep. Bill Thomas
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a committee markup or hearing, so it never reached the House floor

sides.party_line_note: Every one of the 52 cosponsors was a Democrat or the Independent Bernie Sanders; no Republican signed on, and the Ways and Means Committee's Republican chairman never acted on it.

industries.industry: Tax shelter promoters and material advisors (accounting and law firms)
industries.note: The bill would require advisors to disclose shelter clients, strip confidentiality, and stiffen preparer penalties up to $5,000 per understatement, cutting into the fees these firms earn designing and defending aggressive deals [S2][S3].

Penalties for nondisclosure would rise to $100,000–$200,000, understatements from sham deals would carry a 40% penalty with no interest deduction, and stock-acquisition and foreign-subsidiary tax games would be disallowed — meaning more taxes paid that currently come out of a base ordinary taxpayers help carry [S2][S3].

Individuals with over $2 million in net worth would face the elevated nondisclosure penalties and the economic-substance test on business and investment transactions, closing shelters built around their scale [S2][S3].
